body.text: A hobby starts to sound like a line item somewhere between the pottery-studio membership and the camera that needs its own backpack. It doesn't have to. Most of the ones people stick with begin with one small first purchase that makes the first evening nicer.

Below are fifteen, each with the first thing worth getting, a note on cost and a first small step. Treat it as a menu: pick the one that makes you curious and give it a go. A short closing section covers the ones you can try before buying anything.

body.title: Watercolor painting
body.note: A small pan set, one decent brush and a pad of paper will do, and colors blooming into each other is a joy from the very first page. Upgrade the paper once you've filled a dozen pages. [Watercolor painting for beginners](/journal/watercolor-painting-for-beginners) walks through a first session.
body.first: Paint a wash in three colors and let them bleed into each other.

body.title: Junk journaling
body.note: Glue receipts, tickets and the things you'd normally recycle into a notebook. The [beginner's guide](/journal/how-to-start-junk-journaling) walks through the first page. **What makes it easier:** {{product:stationery-island-a5-blank-journal-180-pages|a blank A5 journal}} and a glue stick, so page one starts the moment you spot a ticket stub.
body.first: Glue in one receipt and one ticket, then add a sentence about the day.

body.title: Air-dry clay
body.note: One block of clay and a few acrylic paints will see you through several small projects. No kiln needed, and few special tools. [How to start air-dry clay](/journal/how-to-start-air-dry-clay) covers a first project. **What makes it easier:** a block of air-dry clay and a set of small acrylic craft paints, so a trinket dish goes from pinch to painted in one sitting.
body.first: Pinch a small trinket dish and leave it to dry overnight.

body.title: Paint by numbers
body.note: The no-blank-page way to paint something frame-worthy. Choose a small size over a giant canvas. **What makes it easier:** a small paint-by-number kit with the numbered canvas, paints and a brush in one box; check the listing for what's included.
body.first: Fill in every shape marked with the same number.

body.title: Embroidery
body.note: [How to start embroidery](/journal/how-to-start-embroidery) covers the stitches. Learn three stitches (running, back, satin) and you can make plenty. **What makes it easier:** {{product:bradove-classic-embroidery-kit|a beginner embroidery kit}}, so the hoop, fabric, floss and needle arrive together; check the listing for what's included.
body.first: Stitch the first outline of the pattern.

body.title: Friendship bracelets
body.note: Colorful floss and a safety pin to hold your work in place. Make one for yourself before you start on gifts. **What makes it easier:** a friendship bracelet kit, so the floss, beads and instructions arrive together. Check the label for small parts.
body.first: Learn the forward knot and make a short striped band.

body.title: Outdoor sketching
body.note: A pencil and a small sketchbook. Draw a tree, a bench or your coffee cup. The fancy pencils can wait. **What makes it easier:** a pocket-size sketch pad and a black fineliner ({{product:sakura-pigma-micron-8-pack-black|a pack of black fineliner pens}} is one option), so outlines go down quickly on a bench.
body.first: Draw one object for ten minutes without looking at the paper.

body.title: A first purchase for a making evening
body.dek: A small paint set, a block of clay, an embroidery kit or a bracelet kit each arrive ready to use, so the first evening is about making, not shopping. Start with the one you're most curious about.

body.text: We've left out dollar figures because prices shift with where you live, new versus secondhand and what's on offer, so check local prices before you buy. Online prices also often leave out shipping and tax.

Two habits keep costs down whatever you pick. Borrow first, since your library may lend more than books and a friend may own a hoop or a spare set of paints. And check secondhand: charity shops, swaps and neighborhood groups are full of barely used supplies.

body.title: Jigsaw puzzles
body.note: Secondhand puzzles are everywhere. Check the pieces are all there before you pay, or swap with a friend. **What makes it easier:** a jigsaw puzzle sized to fit your table, so the edge pieces and the frame take shape on the first evening.
body.first: Sort the edge pieces and build the frame.

body.title: Baking
body.note: You probably own most of what a simple batch of cookies or banana bread needs. A mixing bowl and a tray are enough.
body.first: Bake a one-bowl recipe and give half away.

body.title: Indoor gardening
body.note: A cutting from a friend's plant in a jar of water is the easy start. Add a small pot when it grows roots. If you share your home with pets, check plants against the ASPCA's toxic and non-toxic plant list first, because some common houseplants are harmful to pets. **What makes it easier:** a few propagation jars and a small pot, so a cutting has somewhere to sit by the window.
body.first: Take a cutting, put it by a bright window and check it weekly.

body.title: Creative writing
body.note: Ten minutes on anything at all: a memory, a stranger on the bus, tonight's dinner. **What makes it easier:** a pocket notebook that lives in your bag, so a ten-minute scene can happen on the bus or in a café.
body.first: Set a ten-minute timer and write without editing.

body.title: For a cozy evening in
body.dek: A puzzle for the coffee table, jars for a cutting, a pocket notebook and a clip-on light make a quiet night feel planned.

body.text: These can start today with what you already own or can borrow, and a small piece of gear makes each one nicer once you're hooked.

body.title: Reading
body.note: Your library card gets you the books, and a clip-on light makes bedtime reading cozier. **What makes it easier:** a rechargeable clip-on book light, so you can keep reading when the room goes dim.
body.first: Borrow three books and read the first twenty pages of each.

body.title: Birdwatching
body.note: Your eyes, a window or a park bench, and a bird-ID app or a library field guide. **Nice to have:** compact binoculars, which bring a bird across the pond right up close once you're hooked.
body.first: Sit for fifteen minutes and note every bird you see.

body.title: Hiking and local walks
body.note: Comfortable shoes, water and a trail near you. Many public trails are free, though some parks charge for parking or entry. **What makes it easier:** walking shoes with grip, a small daypack and a water bottle, so a trail morning is a matter of grabbing a bag.
body.cost: Varies; some parks charge for parking or entry
body.first: Walk a short trail with a friend and turn back at the halfway point.

body.title: Thrifting
body.note: Set a spending cap before you leave, a number you're happy to part with. Look for one thing you'd never buy new. **What makes it easier:** a roomy market tote, so finds ride on your shoulder between shops.
body.first: Visit one secondhand shop, choose one item and go home.

body.title: For your first walk-and-look outing
body.dek: Binoculars, walking shoes, a daypack and a tote turn a local walk into an outing worth repeating.

body.text: Start small, then upgrade what you love

For the craft hobbies, a small kit or set in the smallest size is a lovely first buy: everything arrives in one box and you can start the same evening. Better paper, a nicer brush, binoculars and a trail-ready daypack are the fun upgrades once you've done the hobby a few times and know what you'd enjoy more. Before you order, walk around your home: a notebook, pens, scissors, a glue stick, a mixing bowl, a baking tray, old jars, comfortable shoes and a tote may already be here, which keeps the first order small.

Still stuck choosing? Ask what you want from your evenings. Something for your hands: start with the first list. Something quiet: the second. Something that gets you out the door: the third. The [Hobby Finder quiz](/hobby-finder) narrows it down in a couple of minutes.
